transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 38m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Acme ML - ML Eng), Jordan Reed (Acme ML - Infra), Priya Nair (Acme ML - Product)
Shared: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme-poc-2025-03-05)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy Wednesday. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Maya: Maya here.
[00:08] Jordan: Jordan on infra.
[00:09] Priya: Priya here.
[00:12] Samira: Samira from Redwood.
[00:14] Alex: Cool, objective today is unit economics deep dive — tokens per second per dollar, caching savings we've seen, and batching tradeoffs. We'll kick off with the benchmark highlights then dig into questions.

[02:00] Alex: Quick numbers from the spreadsheet - baseline (hosted shared pool) averages about 350 tokens/sec for the 3B-ish model on sample workload, p95 latency ~220ms, and our cost calc gives roughly 8,300 tokens/sec per $1 (derived from $0.12 per 1k tokens). That's the baseline for comparisons.
[02:38] Maya: Wait, can you repeat the tokens/sec/$ calc? I want to make sure we're all using same metric.
[02:44] Samira: Yeah - so we compute tokens/sec/$ as (measured tokens/sec) divided by cost per second. Cost per second we derive from $ per token, where $0.12 per 1k tokens => $0.00012 per token. So for 350 tokens/sec cost per sec ~0.042, tokens/sec/$ ~= 350 / 0.042 ~= 8.3k. I realize it sounds odd but it normalizes throughput to spend.

[05:10] Jordan: That's helpful. Show us the dedicated numbers again — we saw a big improvement last week.
[05:18] Alex: Dedicated A100-equivalent results: we measured 2,200 tokens/sec average (same traffic profile), p95 ~140ms, and because dedicated capacity has amortized lower $/GPU-hour for committed pools, tokens/sec/$ goes up to about 36k in our model (roughly 4.3x improvement). This assumes your committed monthly commit and the Redwood Dedicated pricing tier we discussed.

[07:02] Priya: Good, that 4x figure matters for our CFO. Is that before or after caching?
[07:08] Samira: Those dedicated numbers are pre-cache; we then tested prefix/KV cache on top. With the prefix cache enabled for common prompts (we saw a 42% cache hit rate on the sample set), the effective token generation dropped ~35% overall because many tokens were served from cache. That translates to an incremental cost reduction of about 30-38% depending on hit-rate variance.

[09:35] Maya: 42% hit rate sounds high — is that realistic for our user flows? Our product has lots of short prompts but also long, novel ones.
[09:45] Samira: Right — the sample includes templated prompts which drive higher hit rate. For mixed traffic we ran a synthetic mix (60/40 templated/novel) and saw ~28% hit rate, still meaningful. The spreadsheet has slides 4-6 with the sensitivity analysis.

[12:00] Alex: Important to call out caching tradeoffs: prefix cache reduces tokenized output generation (so lower per-token spend), but it can increase memory pressure on the serving nodes (KV cache size) and may impact cold-start latency when caches repopulate. For Acme's scenario we recommended a warmed cache strategy during peak hours.

[14:20] Jordan: On memory pressure - if we run dedicated with bigger KV cache, what's the cost delta?
[14:26] Samira: Bigger KV cache means fewer misses => higher hit rate but you need more memory per replica which can reduce the number of replicas per GPU, so you may need more GPUs to maintain concurrency. Our model factors that in: for Acme, moving from default 4GB KV to 12GB KV increased infra unit cost by ~12% but improved hit rate from 28% to 36%, net cost improvement ~8% after considering extra nodes.

[16:50] Maya: Let's talk batching — we saw the config you suggested improved tokens/sec but hurt p95 for interactive flows.
[16:58] Samira: Correct. For throughput-oriented endpoints, batching window 40-60ms gave 18-25% better tokens/sec/$ because we increased average batch size. But for interactive flows where p95 latency target is 200ms, that batching window added ~35-50ms to p95 at the p99 tail in some tests. So it's a tradeoff: if you can budget slightly higher latency it's a win for cost. If not, we tune to lower batching windows and accept higher cost.

[19:30] Alex: Example: with batching=50ms we saw tokens/sec rise from 350 -> 480 on shared, and cost per token fell ~16% — tokens/sec/$ up accordingly — but p95 moved from 220ms -> 270ms.

[21:10] Priya: For our product the user experience team wants p95 < 250ms for core interactions. So that suggests we can use moderate batching but need p95 guardrails. Can Redwood do adaptive batching?

[21:22] Samira: Yes — we have dynamic batching policies that prioritize latency-sensitive routes. You can set per-route SLOs and Redwood will trade batch sizes across routes. For example, route A (chat) gets batching window capped at 30ms while route B (background summarization) can go to 80ms. We recommended partitioning routes accordingly.

[23:00] Jordan: Any numbers on quantization/8-bit? We have constrained GPU memory on prem nodes.

[23:06] Samira: Quantization to int8 (or 4-bit in some models) reduces memory footprint substantially; for the 13B-style models we tested int8 gave ~40% memory reduction and ~12% cost improvement overall as it allowed higher packing density. Latency impact was minimal on newer kernels, but some kernels still show a 3-10% p95 degradation. For your 3B baseline it's less material but helps if you want to pack more replicas per GPU on private infra.

[25:40] Maya: The spreadsheet link — is it live with raw logs?
[25:45] Alex: Yes - the benchmark sheet has tabs: raw logs, summarized tokens/sec/$, cache sensitivity, batching matrix. Link in chat: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme-poc-2025-03-05 (shared).

[27:10] Priya: On forecasting — can you provide recommended committed capacity ranges for Q2 to reach our 99th percentile latency target and cost target?
[27:20] Alex: We provided a capacity plan in tab 'capacity-plan'. High level: to keep p95 < 200ms for 95% of traffic and hit target cost per 1M tokens we recommend starting with a 2x committed pool (estimated 4 A100-equivalent units) for pilot ramp to 200 reqs/sec, with autoscale for bursts. That maps to the dedicated pricing scenarios in the sheet. We'll include scenario 1/2/3 with different commit levels.

[29:40] Maya: For the pilot, what's the ideal split of traffic to route to dedicated vs hosted?
[29:48] Samira: Operationally we suggest 10-20% of production traffic to dedicated initially for Canary and benchmarks (this gives signal on hit rates, batch behavior). Then ramp to 50% once cache warms and tail latency stabilizes. The routing policy can be by route or by user cohort.

[31:12] Jordan: Any gotchas on SLOing and fallback? We don't want user-facing errors if dedicated outages occur.

[31:20] Samira: Redwood supports automatic fallback to hosted pool or smaller model variants. We recommend a policy where critical routes fall back to a smaller low-latency model with preserved semantics rather than blocking requests; those fallbacks are in the 'rollout' tab.

[33:40] Alex: Quick product note — we can instrument token-level cost breakdown by route so you can see tokens/sec/$ in the console per route and per user cohort. That'll help the product team run cost experiments.

[34:50] Priya: Good — CFO wants to see a 3-4 month runway for cost improvements before committing.
[34:56] Alex: Understood. That's why we gave staged commit scenarios.

[36:00] Alex: Ok let's recap action items and next steps.
[36:07] Maya: Quick q — can Samira include recommended cache TTLs for our templated prompts?
[36:12] Samira: Yes — I'll add TTL recommendations per route (short TTL for dynamic user prompts, longer TTL for templated system prompts).

[36:30] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll send the updated spreadsheet and a short note summarizing the recommended batching/profile per route. If no other questions, we'll adjourn.
[36:40] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[36:42] Jordan: Thanks.
[36:44] Maya: Thanks, bye.
